title: Quantifying the parent's informal exponential-rate claim
content: The parent entry (leibniz-pi-oq-01) proves the Leibniz/arctan series at $x=1$ converges at the sharp boundary rate $\Theta(1/N)$ and *asserts* that 'Machin-type formulas achieve exponential $O(1/m^{2N})$ rates instead.' This entry turns that assertion into a theorem: for every $0 \le x < 1$ the truncation error of the arctangent power series is bounded by the single geometric quantity $x^{2N+1}/(1-x^2)$, which is $O((x^2)^N)$. The Leibniz slowdown is exactly the $x \to 1$ degeneration of this bound, where $(1-x^2)^{-1}$ diverges.
mathContext: $\arctan x = \sum_n (-1)^n x^{2n+1}/(2n+1)$; truncation error $\le x^{2N+1}/(1-x^2)$ for $0 \le x < 1$.

title: The series term and its partial sum
content: Two definitions fix the objects under study. `arctanTerm x n` is the $n$-th term $(-1)^n x^{2n+1}/(2n+1)$ exactly as it appears in Mathlib's `Real.hasSum_arctan`, and `arctanPartial x N` is the $N$-term truncation $\sum_{n<N}$ of those terms. Matching the term shape to the library lemma verbatim is what lets the later proof invoke `Real.hasSum_arctan` without any re-indexing. Both are `noncomputable` because they live over the reals.

title: Dropping the 1/(2n+1) factor: term domination
content: `abs_arctanTerm_le` shows $|a_n| \le x^{2n+1}$ for $x \ge 0$: since $2n+1 \ge 1$, dividing by $(2n+1)$ only shrinks the magnitude ($\texttt{div\_le\_self}$). Stripping the sign ($|(-1)^n|=1$) and the harmonic denominator is the single approximation in the whole argument — it replaces the alternating arctangent series by a plain geometric majorant, trading a delicate cancellation-based bound for a robust term-by-term one.

title: The series converges to arctan on [0,1)
content: `hasSum_arctanTerm` specialises Mathlib's `Real.hasSum_arctan` (valid for $\|x\|<1$) to the range $0 \le x < 1$, rewriting the norm hypothesis via $\|x\| = |x| = x$. This is the analytic input that identifies the infinite sum of `arctanTerm` with the actual value $\arctan x$, so that a bound on the tail becomes a bound on the truncation error.

title: The dominating geometric tail in closed form
content: `hasSum_geom_tail` computes the majorant series exactly: $\sum_{i} x^{2(i+N)+1} = x^{2N+1}(1-x^2)^{-1}$. The trick is to factor each tail power as $x^{2N+1}\cdot(x^2)^i$ (the rewrite $2(i+N)+1 = (2N+1)+2i$ with `pow_add`/`pow_mul`), reducing to the standard geometric series $\sum_i (x^2)^i = (1-x^2)^{-1}$ scaled by the constant $x^{2N+1}$. Providing the *closed-form* sum — not just convergence — is what makes the final error bound an explicit, computable quantity.

title: Remainder as a shifted HasSum, then geometric comparison
content: The main theorem `arctan_series_error_bound`. Its crux is `hasSum_nat_add_iff'`, which identifies the partial-sum remainder $\arctan x - \mathrm{arctanPartial}(x,N)$ with a genuine infinite sum $\sum_i a_{i+N}$ of the *shifted* sequence — converting a finite-truncation statement into an infinite-sum comparison. `tsum_of_norm_bounded` then closes it: each shifted term is dominated by $x^{2(i+N)+1}$ (via `abs_arctanTerm_le`), and the dominating series sums to the closed form $x^{2N+1}(1-x^2)^{-1}$. The result is exponential decay $O((x^2)^N)$ for every $x<1$.

title: Machin's exponential advantage as a corollary
content: Rewriting $\pi/4 = 4\arctan(1/5) - \arctan(1/239)$ (Mathlib's `four_mul_arctan_inv_5_sub_arctan_inv_239`) and splitting the error with the triangle inequality ($|4a-b| \le 4|a|+|b|$) yields an explicit two-term bound on the $N$-term Machin truncation error. Because the dominant term decays like $(1/5)^{2N}$, each additional term buys a fixed number of decimal digits — the precise sense in which Machin (1706) beat the Leibniz series, and the classical basis of high-precision $\pi$ computation before the modern AGM/spigot era.
